dissipate
proliferate

questions.passage: In the 2010s, the price of vintage empty soda cans rose dramatically, which had the counterintuitive effect of _____ demand: buyers who hadn’t previously wanted to purchase old soda cans suddenly thronged the market, believing prices would continue to rise and the cans could be resold later at a profit.

choices: exploiting
precipitating
stabilizing
monetizing
questions.why: Rising prices brought in new buyers, so they set off (precipitated) demand; that is the counterintuitive part.

It describes how authors write novels.

It explains what a debut novel is.

questions.passage: Archaeologist Yijie Zhuang and colleagues uncovered a network of ceramic pipes and drainage ditches in China that date back to the Longshan period (about 4,000 years ago). The system’s complexity would have required a highly advanced level of community-wide planning, but there is no evidence of a centralized authority that could have overseen such planning. The intricacy of the network refutes the common view that only a centralized governing power would be able to gather the resources to build such a complex water-management system.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a discovery made by Zhuang and colleagues, notes important contextual information about that discovery, and then explains a potential implication of that discovery and contextual information.
It introduces an unusual aspect of an ancient water system in China, offers a hypothesis about how that aspect came to be, and then signals future research that might bolster that hypothesis.
It summarizes a conclusion reached by Zhuang and colleagues, acknowledges a counterargument to that conclusion, and then refutes that counterargument with additional evidence.

It highlights an ancient water-management system discovered in China, points out a significant feature of that system, and then provides additional information clarifying the function of that feature.
questions.why: Discovery (the pipe network), context (needs planning, yet no central authority), implication (refutes the common view).
flags: Stem cut off in the screenshot; 'overall structure' stem inferred from the choices.
Watermark replaced a word: 'gather the ___ to build'. 'resources' is a placeholder pending the user.

questions.passage: Information from the Great Sunflower Project helps scientists address pollinator population-size declines caused by habitat loss. Participants monitor which pollinators visit specific plants and the frequency of those visits. Scientists then use this information to determine which plant species best support pollinators and identify where those plant species have declined. Without bees, butterflies, and other pollinators performing their vital role in plant reproduction and food production, ecosystems would suffer—making the conservation efforts informed by this citizen science project all the more important!
questions.stem: According to the text, why is the information collected by the Great Sunflower Project valuable?
choices: It helps scientists determine which flowers produce the most honey when visited by bees.
It helps project participants demonstrate that butterfly population sizes are growing faster than bee population sizes.
It helps gardeners learn how to grow larger sunflowers through better pollination.
It helps scientists develop strategies for addressing pollinator habitat loss.
questions.why: The first sentence: the information helps scientists address declines caused by habitat loss.
flags: Watermark replaced the dash in 'suffer—making'; restored.

questions.passage: In her history of the US Civil Rights Movement, Tomiko Brown-Nagin notes that much of the NAACP’s national agenda in the 1950s was shaped by the progressive ideas of the organization’s New York–based lawyers, who argued civil rights cases in federal courts on behalf of clients in distant locations, mostly in the South. Meanwhile, the efforts of NAACP branch leaders in the South, such as A.T. Walden in Atlanta, were made alongside community members, many of whom were business owners, educators, or health care workers. Like Walden, they tended to favor conservative social values and an approach to civil rights work suited to local circumstances.
questions.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the NAACP in the 1950s?
choices: Local organizers realized that a unified strategy for the organization as a whole would have to take into account their approaches as well as those of the lawyers based in New York.
Political disagreements among prominent community organizers negatively affected the organization’s ability to undertake civil rights campaigns in Atlanta.
The organization’s national priorities were influenced by individuals who had less direct contact with the people they represented than did A.T. Walden and other local organizers.

Unlike A.T. Walden and other Atlanta residents, who favored community-based efforts, the organization’s staff in New York believed that federal courts offered the most effective route to securing civil rights.
questions.why: The national agenda came from New York lawyers representing distant clients, while local leaders worked alongside their communities.
flags: Watermark replaced the verb: 'lawyers, who ___ civil rights cases'. 'argued' is a placeholder pending the user.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Nathaniel Hawthorne’s 1830 short story “Sir William Phips.”

The knowledge, communicated by the historian and biographer, is analogous to that which we acquire of a country by the map,—minute, perhaps, and accurate, and available for all necessary purposes, but cold and naked, and wholly destitute of the mimic charm produced by painting. These defects are partly remediable, and even without an absolute violation of literal truth, although by methods rightfully interdicted to professors of biographical exactness.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Historians’ fidelity to the truth often results in work that is less engaging than it could be.
Maps are more practical to own than paintings.
Historians do not agree among themselves about the best methods of recording history.
Biographers are more-skilled writers than other kinds of historians.
questions.why: History is accurate like a map but cold, lacking a painting's charm; the fix uses methods barred to those bound to exactness.

questions.passage: Variously, researchers have closely examined obsidian artifacts to map ancient economic and cultural exchange routes, as in David V. Burley and colleagues’ 2011 study, or to glean aspects of cultural identity, as in Dennis Ogburn and colleagues’ 2009 study. Studies of the Malia archaeological site on the Mediterranean island of Crete have shown that significant changes to building styles—changes consistent with an influx of people from another culture elsewhere in the Mediterranean—occurred from the Middle Bronze Age to the Late Bronze Age. In a 2022 study, however, Tristan Carter and Vassilis Kilikoglou found that obsidian-object production methods at Malia stayed remarkably consistent during this architectural transition, which they interpret as indicative of local cultural continuity in the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Carter and Kilikoglou’s argument?
choices: Changes to buildings like those that occurred at Malia have not been linked to changes in obsidian-object production methods in other Mediterranean cultures during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.
The methods used to produce obsidian objects at Malia during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages were also used by some other Mediterranean cultures in the period.
The obsidian-object production method that was most common among other Mediterranean cultures during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages was more efficient than the method used at Malia.
The obsidian used to produce objects at Malia was transported to Crete from the same source elsewhere in the Mediterranean throughout the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.
questions.why: If newcomers from elsewhere used the same methods, unchanged methods no longer show the local culture continued.
flags: Watermark covered 'Carter' and 'object'; restored from the stem and choice C.

questions.passage: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology is increasingly prevalent in online marketing, largely in the form of autonomously operating algorithms that make use of extensive collections of data about individuals’ behavior to generate highly personalized advertisements in real time. In a recent survey of college students’ attitudes toward AI marketing, researchers found that respondents expressed little concern about AI marketing technology in general but expressed a high degree of concern about the collection and use of personal data (be it their own or other people’s). Since machine learning on immense troves of such data is intrinsic to the functionality of AI marketing tools, this discrepancy suggests that _____
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the college students included in the survey may not be representative of the general population with regard to attitudes toward AI marketing technology.
respondents’ attitudes toward AI marketing technology in general may be a result of the respondents having a limited understanding of how that technology works.
respondents have little concern about the collection and use of personal data in the abstract but are uncomfortable with their own data being collected and used.
the potential drawbacks of AI marketing technology influence respondents’ attitudes more than do the potential benefits of that technology.
questions.why: They worry about data use but not about AI, which is built on data use: they likely don't understand how it works.
flags: Watermark covered 'that' in 'algorithms that make use'; restored.
Inference must stay the last reading question: the cut-off Q15 (support finding) goes before this one.

Delight.” However,
Delight” however

questions.passage: In 2020, internationally renowned Slovak photographer Mária Švarbová exhibited her work at the Contessa Gallery and the Art Angel Gallery in the United States and _____ utilizing vivid pastel colors, overexposed tones, and mirror like symmetry, Švarbová’s photographs evoke a Socialist-era aesthetic that she describes as “minimalistic but also futuristic.”

Japan, respectively

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Uzbek is a language in the Turkic language family.
  • In Uzbek, a noun takes a different form when that noun functions as a location in a sentence.
  • The Uzbek noun xona (room) is combined with the locative suffix -da to become the locative noun xonada (in the room).
  • Danish is a language in the Germanic language family.
  • In Danish, nouns do not change form to indicate location.
  • In Danish, nouns used as a location must be indicated by prepositions such as i (in) or på (on).
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between Uzbek and Danish nouns. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Though nouns in Uzbek change form to indicate location, this Turkic language belongs to a different language family than Danish does.
To indicate location in Uzbek, a suffix is appended to a noun, but in Danish, the noun is unchanged and a preposition is used.
In Uzbek, nouns take a different form when they function as a location, as the language belongs to the Turkic family; Danish, however, belongs to the Germanic family.
Uzbek and Danish belong to two distinct language families; the former is in the Turkic family, while the latter is a Germanic language.
questions.why: Only B contrasts the nouns themselves: a suffix in Uzbek, an unchanged noun plus a preposition in Danish. A, C and D contrast the language families.
flags: Watermark covered the locative noun; restored as 'xonada' (xona + -da).

questions.passage:

Sherman claims that period maps of the UK present “a powerful visual representation” of how the country’s rural landscape was transformed by population shifts during the Industrial Revolution.

Sherman claims that maps of Industrial Revolution–era Manchester, England, present “a powerful visual representation of the transformation of Manchester’s landscape” during a time period in which the UK experienced a substantial (2,000%) increase in population.

The sizeable growth in the UK’s urban population during the Industrial Revolution is reflected in before-and-after maps that present, in Sherman’s view, “a powerful visual representation” of how the increase transformed Manchester.
questions.why: D ties the UK's urban growth to Sherman's maps of Manchester accurately. A and B misdescribe what the quotation is about; C puts Manchester's 2,000% on the whole UK.
